title: Atomic Structure
summary: ## The atom is divisible

Dalton's atomic theory (1803) treated the atom as the smallest, indivisible particle; it explained the laws of conservation of mass, constant proportions and multiple proportions. Experiments at the end of the nineteenth century showed that atoms are made of still smaller subatomic particles — electrons (negative), protons (positive) and neutrons (no charge). Radioactivity also showed that atoms can break up.
## Discovery of the electron

A cathode ray tube is a partly evacuated glass tube with two electrodes, the cathode (−) and anode (+), joined to a high voltage. At very high voltage the cathode gives out cathode rays that travel to the anode. J.J. Thomson (1897) showed that they are streams of negatively charged particles, later called electrons. Properties of cathode rays: they travel in straight lines; the particles have mass and kinetic energy but very small mass and high speed; they carry negative charge and bend towards the positive plate in an electric field; their nature and charge-to-mass ratio (e/m) are the same whatever the gas or the metal of the electrodes — so all atoms contain electrons.
## Discovery of the proton

Eugen Goldstein (1886) used a perforated cathode in a tube with gas at low pressure and saw a red glow behind the cathode, caused by anode rays (positive rays or canal rays) moving opposite to cathode rays. They travel in straight lines, are much heavier than electrons and carry positive charge in whole-number multiples of the electronic charge; their nature depends on the gas. They form when cathode rays knock electrons out of gas atoms. With hydrogen the particles were lightest with the highest e/m; Rutherford showed they are hydrogen ions and named them protons.
## Thomson's model

Thomson's 'plum pudding' model: the atom is a sphere of uniform positive charge in which negatively charged electrons are scattered, like seeds in a water-melon; the total positive and negative charges are equal, so the atom is neutral.
## Rutherford's α-scattering experiment and model

Geiger and Marsden (1910) directed α-particles (helium nuclei) at a very thin gold foil. Most α-particles went straight through, some were deflected by small angles, a few by large angles, and about 1 in 12 000 bounced back. Rutherford (1911) explained this with the nuclear model: a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus at the centre contains all the positive charge and almost all the mass; the rest of the atom is mostly empty space in which the electrons move around the nucleus (like planets round the Sun). The nucleus is about 10 000 times smaller than the atom — like a fly in a cricket stadium.

Drawbacks: a revolving charged electron should lose energy continuously and spiral into the nucleus, so the model cannot explain the stability of the atom; it says nothing about how electrons are arranged; and it cannot explain why the atomic mass is more than the mass of the protons (e.g. helium is four times as heavy as hydrogen).
## Bohr's model (1913)

Postulate 1: electrons move only in certain circular orbits of fixed energy (energy levels or stationary states) around the nucleus, and while in an orbit an electron does not radiate energy — this explains the stability of the atom. The orbits are later called shells, three-dimensional regions K, L, M, N (n = 1, 2, 3, 4), with energy increasing outwards. Postulate 2: an electron changes its level only by absorbing or emitting energy equal to the difference between the levels (E = hν = Ef − Ei).
## The neutron

James Chadwick (1932) discovered the neutron — a neutral particle with a mass slightly more than a proton, present in the nucleus of every atom except ordinary hydrogen. It explains the 4 : 1 mass ratio of helium to hydrogen (2 protons + 2 neutrons). The electron's mass (9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg) is about 1/1840 of a proton's; electron charge −1, proton +1, neutron 0. An α-particle contains 2 protons and 2 neutrons.
## Atomic number and mass number

Atomic number Z = number of protons = number of electrons in a neutral atom; it is what makes one element different from another. Protons and neutrons are called nucleons; mass number A = protons + neutrons. An element is written with A as a superscript and Z as a subscript, e.g. ¹²₆C has 6 protons, 6 electrons and 6 neutrons; ²³₁₁Na has 11 protons, 11 electrons, 12 neutrons; ⁴⁰₁₈Ar has 22 neutrons and ⁴⁰₁₉K has 21.
## Electronic configuration

Bohr–Bury rules: shells K, L, M, N (n = 1, 2, 3, 4) are filled in order of increasing energy; the maximum number of electrons in a shell is 2n² (K 2, L 8, M 18, N 32); a new shell is started only when the inner one is full (for the first 18 elements the outermost shell holds at most 8). Examples: H 1; He 2; Li 2,1; C 2,4; N 2,5; O 2,6; Ne 2,8; Na 2,8,1; Mg 2,8,2; Al 2,8,3; P 2,8,5; S 2,8,6; Cl 2,8,7; Ar 2,8,8; K 2,8,8,1; Ca 2,8,8,2.
## Valency

Electrons in the outermost shell are valence electrons; they decide the combining capacity (valency) — the number of bonds an atom forms with univalent atoms such as hydrogen (O in H2O is 2, N in NH3 is 3, C in CH4 is 4). Atoms with a full outer shell (He, Ne, Ar) have valency 0 and are unreactive. Valency = number of valence electrons if it is 4 or less; otherwise valency = 8 − number of valence electrons (octet rule). For example, O (2,6) has valency 2 and Cl (2,8,7) has valency 1.

vsa: Describe J.J. Thomson's plum-pudding model of the atom and give one limitation of this model.

Thomson pictured the atom as a sphere of uniform positive charge with electrons scattered in it like plums in a pudding (or seeds in a water-melon), the total charges being equal. Limitation: it could not explain the results of the α-scattering experiment — some α-particles were deflected through large angles, which needs a small, concentrated positive nucleus.

October 2025
Write any two postulates proposed by Niels Bohr in his model of the atom.

(1) Electrons move around the nucleus only in certain circular orbits (energy levels) of fixed energy, and while moving in an orbit they do not lose energy (stationary states). (2) An electron can jump from one level to another only by absorbing or emitting energy equal to the difference in the energies of the two levels (E = hν).
April 2024

or: State any two results of the α-ray scattering experiment explained by Rutherford.

(1) Most α-particles passed straight through the foil, so most of the atom is empty space. (2) A few were deflected through large angles or bounced back, so the positive charge and mass are concentrated in a tiny nucleus at the centre.

vsa: An element X has an atomic number of 8. How many valence electrons does it have? What is its valency?
Electronic configuration of X (oxygen) = 2, 6. It has 6 valence electrons. Since this is more than 4, valency = 8 − 6 = 2.
October 2025
Write two differences between an electron and a proton.

(1) An electron carries a negative charge (−1), while a proton carries a positive charge (+1). (2) An electron has very small mass (about 1/1840 of a proton) and moves around the nucleus, while a proton is heavy and is found in the nucleus.
October 2024
Write two differences between an electron and a neutron.

(1) An electron is negatively charged, while a neutron has no charge. (2) An electron is very light and moves outside the nucleus, while a neutron has a mass slightly more than a proton and is found inside the nucleus.
April 2025
A sodium atom has atomic number 11 and mass number 23. Find the number of protons, electrons and neutrons in it.
Protons = atomic number = 11; electrons = 11 (the atom is neutral); neutrons = mass number − atomic number = 23 − 11 = 12.
Why did Thomson conclude that all atoms contain electrons?

The cathode rays produced in the discharge tube had the same nature and the same charge-to-mass ratio whatever gas was filled in the tube and whatever metal the electrodes were made of. So the negatively charged particles (electrons) must be present in the atoms of all substances.
sa: Describe Thomson's model of the atom. Draw a diagram of a helium atom according to this model.

Thomson's plum-pudding model: an atom is a sphere of uniformly spread positive charge in which electrons are embedded like plums in a pudding, so that the atom as a whole is neutral. Diagram: a circle (positive sphere) with two dots marked '−' (the two electrons of helium) placed inside it; total positive charge +2 balances the two electrons.

or: Calculate the number of electrons, protons and neutrons in ⁴⁰₁₈Ar and ⁴⁰₁₉K.
⁴⁰₁₈Ar: protons 18, electrons 18, neutrons 40 − 18 = 22. ⁴⁰₁₉K: protons 19, electrons 19, neutrons 40 − 19 = 21.

sa: An element having 13 electrons forms an ion which has 10 electrons and three positive charges. (i) How many protons are there in its ionic form? (ii) What will be its atomic number and mass number if it has 14 neutrons? (iii) What will be the formula of its sulphate?
(i) The number of protons does not change when the ion forms: 13. (ii) Atomic number = 13; mass number = 13 + 14 = 27 (it is aluminium). (iii) Al³⁺ and SO₄²⁻ give Al2(SO4)3.
April 2025
What was the model of the atom proposed by Rutherford after explaining the results of the α-ray scattering experiment in 1911?

(1) An atom has a small, dense, positively charged centre called the nucleus. (2) All the positive charge and almost all the mass of the atom is in the nucleus. (3) The electrons move around the nucleus in the large empty space around it, like planets round the Sun; the nucleus is about 10 000 times smaller than the atom.
October 2024

The atom of an element X has 18 protons in its nucleus. (a) How many electrons are present in its energy shells? Write its electronic configuration. (b) What is the valency of X? Explain its ability to react with other elements.
(a) 18 electrons, arranged 2, 8, 8. (b) Its outermost shell has 8 electrons — a complete octet — so its valency is zero. X (argon) is a noble gas and does not normally react with other elements.
April 2019
Two atoms X and Y are ²⁰₁₀X and ²⁷₁₃Y. What are atomic number and mass number? Find the atomic number and valency of X and Y.

Atomic number is the number of protons in an atom; mass number is the number of protons + neutrons. X: Z = 10, configuration 2, 8 — full outer shell, valency 0. Y: Z = 13, configuration 2, 8, 3 — 3 valence electrons, valency 3.
April 2022
(a) Draw the structure of a phosphorus atom (atomic number 15) according to Bohr's model and write its valency. (b) What happens when an electron of phosphorus moves from the L shell to the M shell?

(a) Nucleus with 15 protons (and 16 neutrons) surrounded by shells K (2 electrons), L (8) and M (5) — configuration 2, 8, 5. With 5 valence electrons its valency is 8 − 5 = 3 (it can also show 5). (b) The M shell has more energy than the L shell, so the electron must absorb a definite amount of energy (equal to the difference in energies) to move from L to M.
October 2016
Describe Thomson's model of the atom and why it was discarded. Who performed the α-ray scattering experiment and what were its main conclusions?

Thomson's model: a sphere of uniform positive charge with electrons embedded in it. It was discarded because it could not explain why a few α-particles were deflected through large angles. The experiment was done by Geiger and Marsden (under Rutherford). Conclusions: most of the atom is empty space; the positive charge and mass are concentrated in a very small nucleus; the nucleus is about 10 000 times smaller than the atom.
October 2021
la: State the postulates of Bohr's model of the atom. How could this model answer the problem of the stability of the atom faced by Rutherford's model? Show the electron distribution of chlorine (Z = 17) and potassium (Z = 19).

Postulates: (1) electrons revolve around the nucleus only in certain circular orbits (energy levels K, L, M …) of fixed energy and do not radiate energy while in them; (2) an electron changes its level only by absorbing or emitting energy equal to the difference between the two levels. Stability: in Rutherford's model a revolving electron should lose energy and spiral into the nucleus; Bohr's stationary orbits mean no energy is lost, so the atom is stable. Chlorine: 2, 8, 7 (K 2, L 8, M 7). Potassium: 2, 8, 8, 1 (K 2, L 8, M 8, N 1).

la.note: October 2022 also asked the difference between a Bohr orbit and an energy shell (an orbit is a two-dimensional circular path; a shell is a three-dimensional region of definite energy), and to distribute the electrons of element A (Z = 10): 2, 8 — valency 0, so it does not react.

la: Describe Rutherford's α-ray scattering experiment with a diagram and write the features of his model of the atom. State its drawbacks.

A beam of α-particles from a radioactive source was directed at a very thin gold foil surrounded by a circular fluorescent screen. Observations: most particles went straight through; some were deflected by small angles; a few by large angles; about 1 in 12 000 bounced back. Model: a tiny, dense, positive nucleus at the centre holding nearly all the mass; electrons revolve around it in the mostly empty space. Drawbacks: a revolving electron should radiate energy and fall into the nucleus, so it cannot explain the atom's stability; it does not explain how electrons are arranged; it cannot explain why atomic mass is more than the mass of the protons (solved by the neutron).

or: How were cathode rays produced using a discharge tube? Give any four properties of cathode rays.

A glass tube with two electrodes is partly evacuated and a very high voltage is applied; rays come from the cathode and travel to the anode. Properties: they travel in straight lines; they consist of particles with mass and kinetic energy; they carry negative charge and bend towards the positive plate in an electric field; their nature and e/m ratio do not depend on the gas or the electrode metal.

la: How are electrons distributed amongst the shells around the nucleus? State the rules and write the configurations of sodium (11) and calcium (20).

Bohr and Bury's rules: (1) shells are named K, L, M, N (n = 1, 2, 3, 4) and are arranged in increasing order of energy; (2) the maximum number of electrons in a shell is 2n² — K 2, L 8, M 18; (3) shells are filled in increasing order of energy; (4) a shell is not occupied until the inner shells are filled (and the outermost shell holds at most 8). Sodium: 2, 8, 1. Calcium: 2, 8, 8, 2.
